items.transcript: Last week, while you were busy researching how to buy emergency rice and beans in bulk, a group of guys who technically aren't supposed to have internet access pulled off the largest theft in human history. A code editor owned by a rocket company spent 11 hours letting anyone SSH into your laptop. A prediction market got robbed in the middle of investigating its own customers for treason. And Anthropic showed that an unreleased Claude model could get root on any unpatched Linux server just by sending it TCP packets. In today's video, we'll break down just another Thursday in this godforsaken hellhole we're trapped in. It is November 3rd, 2026 and you're watching The Code Report. You know, I would love nothing more than to just talk about the latest JavaScript framework, but here we are again. This time, it started last Thursday in the middle of the night when Cursor shipped a new official Claude code extension. Unfortunately, they shipped it without actually knowing they shipped it. The extension would scan your machine for any keys or tokens it could find and then set up a backdoor for attackers to come in later and steal them. It was only up for about 11 hours, but that was still long enough for around 5,000 people to install it. Thankfully, the backdoor required admin rights, which most people don't give to their text editor. So, the blast radius was pretty limited. Meanwhile, around that same time, users on Polymarket started noticing that their funds were being drained simply by logging into the website. Now, this isn't that unusual for Polymarket users, but what was unusual was this time it wasn't their fault. It turns out a script from a company called DebugBear that Polymarket uses for performance monitoring was hijacked to sell all your current positions before wiring the proceeds to a hardcoded wallet. The hackers ended up getting over $2 million worth of funds before Polymarket pulled the script, which seems like a lot until you realize it's just a small price to pay on the road to destroying the lives of millions of young men across the world. Thankfully for Polymarket, the news didn't last long because just a few hours later people started noticing something was up with Binance and it was way worse. In about 20 minutes, 6.3 billion with a B worth of crypto across 10 different blockchains left Binance's hot wallets, which makes this the biggest theft in recorded history. According to Binance, a devops laptop was compromised, which allowed the attackers to submit withdrawal requests, and then Binance's own systems signed them. And the next day, the FBI came out and said they believed that the North Korean group Trader Trader was behind the attack, which was the same group that stole 1.5 billion from Bybit last year. The good news is that if you had money on Binance, is that it stopped being your problem pretty quickly, since crypto isn't actually decentralized. It Tether and Circle froze about 3 billion dollars of the stolen stable coins within an hour, and then Binance froze all withdrawals and spent the weekend refilling its wallets out of its own treasury and insurance funds. But by Sunday, withdrawals were back on, and yesterday they posted proof of reserves showing everyone's balance was fully backed again, to which the users responded by kindly withdrawing 3.6 billion from Binance anyway. And that wasn't even the worst part of the week. But back in early October, a Linux kernel maintainer named Eric Dumazet uh pushed a simple two-line fix that delayed freeing some memory until the kernel is sure nothing is still reading it. At the time, it didn't seem like a big deal, and nobody really paid attention to it until a few weeks later when it got a 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale, which is the industry's way of ranking how bad a security bug is. It turns out that since 2016, every Linux kernel has had a bug in the code that handles new TCP connections. The way it works is every connection starts with the client sending a hello packet, and the server sending one back. Normally, that first packet is pretty uninteresting, but you're allowed to attach a few extra options to it if you want the kernel to save those so it can use them when it builds its reply. The problem is that if the client sends the same hello twice at just the right moment, the two parts of the kernel end up working on the same connection at once, and one of them can free that saved memory while the other one is still reading it. So, the server ends up building its reply out of memory that's already been freed, which means whatever else got written there in the meantime ends up in the reply. And if an attacker controls what that is, they can control what the kernel does next. Now, getting that timing right is pretty tricky, which is why Red Hat initially rated it as a moderate 5.9, and figured the worst-case scenario was that the kernel would just crash because if the exploit only works in one in a million tries, it's basically safe as long as the person trying it gets bored and runs out of money. But, the problem is that world no longer exists, which is exactly what Anthropic proved on October 27th when its red team published a post saying they handed the bug to an unreleased cloud model and in about 48 minutes, the model had hit the timing enough times to get the server to leak a kernel memory address back to it. And just 5 minutes after that, it was able to start running commands as root. Debian and Oracle had patched kernels out within 1 day of the CVE. Red Hat took another 2 weeks to decide it was serious and finally shipped fixes over the weekend. And Ubuntu still doesn't have one, but at least you can protect your own code base with Code Rabbit, the sponsor of today's video.
